title: Congo's Ebola Outbreak Surpasses 4,000 Deaths Amid Violence and Mistrust
summary:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, the health ministry says, as authorities struggle to contain the virus. The latest figures, released on Thursday, show 4,018 deaths among about 8,300 confirmed cases. The outbreak, announced on May 15, is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine. It has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and is now the largest ever recorded in Congo.

Several problems are making the response harder. In Bunia, the capital of Ituri province and the heart of the outbreak, health workers gathered to demand wages they said were owed. Officials quickly dispersed them. Some of the protesters were surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients, and they held signs reading "No money, no data!" Front-line workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began.

Insecurity is also a concern. A senior UN official said soldiers burned an Ebola-hit camp that housed a transit center for infected patients while they were looking for weapons near Bunia. About 19,000 people in the camp had to flee. UN Ebola coordinator Julien Harneis said building transit and treatment centers takes money and staff, which are in short supply. "When we lose a centre, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment and we have to start again," he said.

The disease has also reached aid workers. Doctors Without Borders said one of its aid workers was infected and was flown to the Netherlands for treatment in a high-level isolation unit. The group says more than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus. The World Health Organization has warned that the virus is spreading into new health zones, which stretches limited resources.

There are some signs of change. Confirmed cases have slowed, from around 850 cases and 470 deaths a week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September. Africa CDC says the drop in newly confirmed cases could be attributed to insecurity and difficulty getting communities to cooperate. It says the spread has slowed in some areas but accelerated in others, which experts see as a delicate situation.
why_it_matters: The story shows that stopping a disease depends on more than medicine: health workers need pay, centers need to be safe, and communities need to trust and work with responders.
